1:
Who the angel is divides the chapter's voices more sharply than anything else, and the division is really about what kind of book this is. The oldest witnesses identify him with Christ outright. Victorinus says simply that the mighty angel descending clothed with a cloud is our Lord, reads the face like the sun of the resurrection and the rainbow of the judgment he executes. Bede develops the same reading and makes the cloud a cloud of flesh, citing the prophet's Lord riding on a swift cloud; the brightening face is the knowledge of him made manifest by the resurrection, and the feet are those that preach glad tidings on the mountains, lit with the fire of the Spirit and firm as pillars because James, Cephas and John seemed to be pillars of the Church. Henry reaches the same conclusion in his own idiom, that the description would induce one to think it could be no other than our Lord: the cloud veils a glory too great for mortals and veils his dispensations too, the rainbow shows him always mindful of his covenant even when his conduct is most mysterious, and the feet of fire show that all his ways in grace and providence are pure and steady. Clarke will go only as far as Christ or his representative.

Against them Wesley denies it flatly and gives a reason drawn from further down the chapter: this is a created angel, since he did not swear by himself. He then defends the description attribute by attribute as nothing too great for a creature, observing that the woman of the next vision is more glorious still and the righteous are promised they shall shine forth as the sun. Robertson takes the same side twice over, noting that the cloud is no proof the angel is Christ though Christ will come on the clouds and ascended on one, and that the pillars of fire, close as the figure is to one used of Christ at the book's opening, are still no proof; he calls him rather a special messenger of God, distinct from the seven trumpet angels and from the four.

Gill spends his space clearing away identifications he rejects, and the list is instructive about how the chapter has been read. He dismisses the emperor Justin, whose letters against the Arians some had made the little open book; he dismisses the pope of Rome in both the Catholic and the Protestant construction, the latter making him a tyrant treading on islands and continent and holding out the book of canons and decrees; and he reports without adopting the view that Luther and the reformers are meant, since the chapter is taken to concern the Reformation. Having cleared the ground he refuses a created angel as well.

Barnes belongs to the school Gill reports rather than the one he joins, and states its method openly. He places the vision between the sixth and seventh trumpets, regrets that the chapter division separates what is one continued vision, and argues from the order of events: the previous chapters had, on his reading, brought the history down to the capture of Constantinople and the fall of the Roman empire in the fifteenth century, after which the world was described as unreformed by those judgments, so that the next event to expect is the Reformation. He does not claim the seer understood this, nor that readers before the event could have applied it, only that now the event has occurred the symbols can be shown to fit. On the angel himself he says less than one might expect, taking the strength of him to indicate that the work in hand faced great obstacles and needed great power, and the cloud to be the ordinary accompaniment of the divine presence in the older Scriptures, from which he draws no argument either way about who is meant.
2:
The little book is the hinge of the chapter, and the sources cannot agree what it is. Gill argues it is the very book of the earlier vision, sealed in the hand of him that sat on the throne and opened by the Lamb; since we never read of the Lamb laying it down or handing it on, the angel who now holds it open must be the Lamb himself. He is explicit that it is neither the Bible nor the gospel, though he grants the prophecies here may have respect to the Reformation. Wesley takes a middle position, that this little book contains the remainder of the other and is given opened to John, and draws a consequence: from this point the vision speaks more clearly and less figuratively than before. Robertson keeps the two apart on grammatical grounds, noting the diminutive is a rare form chosen against the ordinary word used of the sealed scroll, and that the large roll was held upon the right hand while this small one is held in it; he locates its contents in the chapter that follows. Clarke declines to decide, saying it means some design of God long concealed and now to be made manifest, but who knows what it means.

Barnes builds his whole reading of the chapter on it. He treats the diminutive as significant, marking this off from the large volume of the earlier vision, its smallness being what makes it possible to hold and afterwards to eat. He then reasons from the emblem: earlier visions gave a bow for conquest, a sword for battle and scales for exact reckoning, so a book, a silent thing meant not to carry desolation but to diffuse light, indicates an age whose characteristic instrument would be a book. Being open matters as much as being small, since the word implies something previously closed: the symbol requires a time when knowledge had been withheld and then became accessible.

Applied, this becomes the Reformation. The moving cause was a book: Wycliffe's English New Testament, suppressed but preparing the people, and Luther's discovery of a Vulgate hidden on the shelves of the university library at Erfurt, until which time he had supposed there were no Gospels or Epistles beyond what the Breviary and the preachers quoted. To that study Barnes traces the whole movement, and he quotes the saying that the Bible is the religion of Protestants. That the book had been shut he supports from the state of the clergy before the Reformation, many unable to read and those with access drawing their doctrine from the Fathers rather than the word of God. If one were now asked to devise an emblem of the Reformation, he concludes, nothing better could be chosen than an angel of benign aspect holding a book out to mankind.

The posture is read with very different confidence. Robertson observes the angel's size must be colossal to bestride land and sea at once, calls it a bold and graphic picture, and says there is apparently no point in which foot rests where. Wesley thinks there is a great deal of point in it. He works out the orientation, the right foot on the sea toward the west and the left on the land toward the east, so the angel faced south, and adds that since Patmos lies near Asia John could conveniently take the book from the left hand, the right being reserved for the oath. He then identifies the elements from later visions, the sea being that out of which the first beast was to come and the earth that which produced the second, and suggests the sea may betoken Europe and the earth Asia, the chief theatres of these great things. Clarke keeps the plainest sense, that the posture shows command of both and a power universal, all things being under his feet.
3:
The cry itself receives little comment because nobody knows what was said. Barnes notes that John made no record of it and refuses to pin it down, since any loud utterance, command or declaration of truth would answer the description equally; he reports one suggestion that it was a note of woe and declines it as unnecessary. Ellicott hears in the roar another token of Christ's presence with the Church, the voice being one of courage drawn from the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Robertson takes the comparison more soberly, glossing the verb as an old word for the bellowing of cattle used by one poet of a lion and another of thunder, and insisting it does not imply the words were unintelligible, only loud. Gill guesses it was the book of prophecy concerning the church.

On the thunders the sources divide four ways, and the argument runs through the definite article. Ellicott insists on translating the seven thunders rather than seven thunders, since the phrase presents them as a further order of sevens beside the seals, trumpets and vials, making four such sets; and he stresses this was not a sevenfold peal but seven distinct voices. Barnes builds the same observation into a longer argument, canvassing the editors who keep or drop the article and concluding the best texts retain it in both places, so the number must be specific rather than the round number the book uses elsewhere. Robertson agrees they form a recognised group that John seems to assume his readers know, and recalls the psalm in which the Lord speaks in the sevenfold voice of a thunderstorm over the sea.

What they were is another matter. Bede identifies them outright with the seven trumpets, one of the two guesses Ellicott says can hardly be admitted, the other being the seven crusades; Ellicott will venture only that they may have been more terrible judgments still, whose sealing would answer to the shortening of the days. Barnes, having established that the number is specific, applies it to Rome: the city of seven hills, whose condemnatory decrees were commonly called papal thunders, and whose anathemas against the Reformers came as a response to the angel's cry just as the thunders here follow it. He supports it from the sequence of his scheme, from the ordinary name for those bulls, and from a writer on Wycliffe who spoke of thunders shaking the world as they issued from the seven hills.

The command to seal is handled with more agreement and more restraint. Robertson observes that John was on the point of beginning to write, as he had been told at the outset, and that both imperatives are urgent, seal at once and do not begin; he calls it idle to conjecture what the utterances contained, and compares the silence of Paul about what he heard in paradise. Ellicott makes the same point about the writing, that what John heard was no mere thunder-like noise but articulate speech he could have taken down, and draws from the prohibition that the utterances were meant for those who heard them and not to be made generally known. He develops this into the chapter's most sustained image: in the Gospel the crowd said it thundered and some thought an angel had spoken, while there were articulate words Christ heard, so dull ears hear thunder and never the voice of God. Wesley notes this is the only thing in the vision John is told to keep secret, so something peculiarly secret was revealed to him beyond all that is written, and we are thereby prevented from inquiring what it was. Henry says as much in a sentence, that we know neither the subjects of the thunders nor the reason for suppressing them, and that there are great events in history, perhaps concerning the church, which open prophecy does not notice.
5:
The gesture is read as a formal one. Robertson notes the upraised hand toward heaven is the customary posture for a solemn oath and cites three older instances; Barnes says the same and adds that heaven is called to witness. Wesley presses further, observing that of the seven trumpets only the seventh is confirmed by an oath, and reading the stance as deliberately comprehensive: since the dragon was as yet in heaven and would bring the third woe on earth and sea when cast down, posture and oath together take in heaven, sea and land, so the protest is made against every quarter where enemies remain. He also notices that the angel in Daniel, whom he thinks may be the same, lifted both hands.

The oath settles a question raised at the opening of the chapter. Robertson states it flatly, that swearing by him that liveth for ever proves this angel is not Christ, which is exactly the argument Wesley had used earlier in denying the identification. Gill explains the formula rather than the inference: the living God is so described to distinguish him from idols that have no breath, and to assert that he has life in himself, independently, as the fountain of life to every creature. Wesley draws the consequence from the mention of creation: one who made heaven, earth and sea has sovereign power over all, so enemies raging for a while in any of the three must give place.

What the oath declares is disputed, and the two readings are old. Henry sets them side by side without choosing: either there shall be no longer delay in fulfilling the book's predictions once the last angel sounds, or else, when the mystery is finished, time itself shall be no more, being the measure of things in a mutable state, so that all is fixed for ever and time swallowed up in eternity. Robertson allows only the first: the expression does not mean time will cease to exist but that there will be no more delay in the fulfilment of the seventh trumpet, in answer to the question how long. Barnes reads it the same way, as a denial that the time had yet come.

That denial is the point of his exposition, and he turns it against the expectations of his own tradition. He documents how general the belief in an imminent end was among the Reformers: a manuscript note in Melancthon's hand in Luther's own copy of the German Bible, reckoning the age of the world and concluding that this aged world is not far from its end; and Latimer, who took the world to have been ordained to endure six thousand years, computed that only some hundreds remained, urged that the falling away foretold by Paul was past and Antichrist already known, and preached that the day might come in his own or his children's time. On his reading the angel's oath answers precisely such anticipations, declaring they would not yet be realised and that a series of events must intervene before the end.

Wesley does the opposite with the same clause, and takes it as licence for a calculation. He treats the phrase as technical, so what is denied is not time in general but a chronos, a period he reckons at rather more than eleven centuries, and infers that a shorter interval, a non-chronos, must run out before the mystery is fulfilled. He then dates it: beginning in the year 800, when Charles the Great instituted a new line of emperors in the west, and ending in 1836, a span containing the short time of the third woe, the three times and a half of the woman in the wilderness, and the duration of the beast. Set beside Barnes, who quotes the Reformers' arithmetic only to show that the verse forbids it, the two readings make the sharpest opposition in the chapter.
7:
What the finished mystery is draws four answers and one refusal. Barnes takes it for the divine purpose long concealed respecting the destiny of the world, unfolded piecemeal through the prophets and consummated at the seventh trumpet, and builds a structural claim on it: that trumpet closes this whole series of visions, after which a new series begins covering the same ground in its ecclesiastical aspect. Robertson glosses it as the whole purpose of God in human history, recalling that the older prophets hoped for a clearing up of all mysteries in the last days. Gill fills it with content, making this the thousand years of Christ's kingdom on earth, a period of unspeakable light after the darkness spread by early heresies, by the Goths and Huns and Vandals when they broke into the empire, and by the smoke of the pit. Wesley distinguishes two things usually run together, the word of God fulfilled by the destruction of the beast and the mystery by the removal of the dragon, so near in time that they are named as one, and adds that the oath is meant to comfort holy men afflicted under the third woe.

Clarke will have none of it, and his refusal is the sharpest thing in the chapter. What the mystery refers to, he asks, who knows; on these points there is little agreement among learned men, and whether the meaning is the destruction of Jerusalem, or of the papal power, or something else, we do not know. He then adds the rebuke: and yet with what confidence do men speak of the meaning of these hidden things. His own tentative suggestion, offered as no more than likely, is that the trumpet belongs to the Jewish state.

The order to eat the book is agreed to be figurative and is variously moralised. Barnes insists the action is symbolic, since one no more supposes a literal journey and meal than a literal angel bestriding sea and land, and compares the same command in Ezekiel, the prophet who found God's words and did eat them, and the Latin verbs for devouring knowledge. Clarke reduces it to a sentence, that John was to comprehend the meaning fully and study it thoroughly. Robertson notices that the ordinary word for book is used when the command is given, where the diminutive stands in the surrounding verses.

Barnes finds his reading confirmed in the manner of the handing over. There was no reluctance in the angel, no attempt to withhold and no hesitation at the first request; and he asks whether the readiness with which God puts his Bible into the hands of men, set against all human efforts to restrain its circulation, would not be well symbolised by such an act.

Henry draws the lesson that the chapter's own structure suggests. The command to eat comes before the command to prophesy, hinting that the messenger must digest what he has discovered and be suitably affected by it before publishing. The taste follows: sweet at first, since all take pleasure in looking into future events and good men welcome any word from God, but bitter when digested, because the things foreseen were grievous persecutions and desolations, so that foreknowledge of them would be painful rather than pleasant, exactly as the like prophecy was to Ezekiel. From this Henry takes two duties, that God's servants should digest in their own souls the messages they carry in his name, and that they should deliver every message with which they are charged whether it pleases men or not, since what is least pleasing may be most profitable and no part of the counsel of God may be kept back. Gill adds only that John went as he was bidden, and asks where else one should go for knowledge than to him who has the words of eternal life.
10:
The two tastes are read as one experience. Robertson notes the order of results is now given as actually felt, sweet in the mouth first and bitter afterwards, and that the plainer verb replaces the emphatic one used in the command. Clarke keeps it simple: the roll held some pleasing and some unpleasing intelligence, so that reading of the consolations of God's true worshippers he rejoiced, and reading of the persecutions of the Church he was distressed.

Ellicott takes the verse as a description of what it costs to carry such a message. He sets the sweetness beside Ezekiel, who found his roll as honey, and the psalmist rejoicing in a law sweeter than the honeycomb, and draws a condition of ministry: the man ready to endure bitterness in his fidelity must not only be penetrated by divine teaching but have tasted its sweetness, or however pleasant his words sound they will lack what is as needful to a teacher as to a poet. The bitterness he supplies from elsewhere, since Ezekiel does not mention it, observing what that prophet's fidelity must have cost a man told to arm himself with a flinty determination among thorns and scorpions. It must always be so, he says: the ardour of affection brings men through tribulation and may leave them defamed, and the zeal to free mankind stirs a holy joy until the task looks hopeless. He instances Moses asking why he had been sent, since from his coming to Pharaoh the people had only fared worse, and concludes that those who love their fellow-men most feel this bitterness most, their love making failure hard to bear, and that through this martyrdom of failure the noblest victories are won.

On the closing commission the grammatical points are agreed. Ellicott and Robertson read the verb as an indefinite plural, they say rather than he said, amounting to it was said, and both take the preposition as concerning rather than before or against, so the renewed charge is to prophesy about peoples and kings rather than in their presence. Robertson adds that this is not a new commission but the old one revived, the list of peoples recurring seven times in the book. Ellicott ties the bitterness to that subject: John must tell the story of churches and peoples, priests and princes unmindful of their calling and hating God's purest witnesses, which carries forward to the next vision where two witnesses prophesy mightily and in vain. The end will come and the kingdoms of the world become Christ's, but through persecutions and judgments. Wesley reads the charge as fulfilled at once by the measuring of the temple, a prophecy delivered by action rather than words, and distinguishes the terms: peoples, nations and tongues are contemporary, but the kings, being many, succeed one another, and he lists the kingdoms that arose or changed from the eighth century in Spain, England, Italy and Germany.

Clarke closes the chapter by refusing the whole enterprise and naming what he refuses. Having noted how closely this vision follows Daniel and Ezekiel, whom he thinks the writer keeps continually in view, he says he does not understand these prophecies and will not undertake to explain them, and observes with regret how many learned men have mistaken their way, trifling in solemn things and finding all the trumpets and vials and woes perfectly easy, while nobody grows wiser from their descriptions. On the same ground he rejects the reading of the word for time that construes it as an artificial period of eleven hundred and eleven years, with its half-period and non-period, and says the writer who argued this at length did so to very little purpose. His own view is that the word means delay simply, referring to the end of God's long-suffering toward Jerusalem, since he takes it throughout as probable that the book was written before that city fell.
